catalog_locator: p.6 right column, end of sec. 7 'The Similarities and Differences Between the Affixal Processes in O̩gba and English Languages' (repeated verbatim in sec. 8 'Conclusion', p.7); the suprafix inventory sentence is sec. 6.3 'Suprafixation in O̩gba and English Languages', p.5 right column, with Table 5 (tone/nasalization minimal pairs) p.5 and Table 6 (English stress pairs) p.6
catalog_quote: The suprasegmental features in natural languages are stress, tone, nasalization, intonation, etc. It is noticed that tone and nasalization are the suprafixes in O̩gba. Tone and nasalization are as essential as the phonemic sounds (consonants and vowels) in the language. ... It is noticed that the suprafixes in O̩gba are tone (variation in the pitch of the voice) and nasalization while the suprafix in the English language is stress. In view of that, this study posits that tones are like the segmental phonemes (consonants and vowels) in O̩gba. That is, tones can alter the meaning of words, phrases, clauses and sentences which otherwise are the same in terms of their segmentals. This is because O̩gba is a tone language. On the other hand, English is a stress sensitive language that is wrong placement of stress can result in misinterpretation.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ogba is described as a tone language (lexically and grammatically contrastive tone: high, low, falling, downstep per Blench 2013; two tones plus downstep per Comparative Igboid) in which stress plays no contrastive/morphological role; stress is attributed to English only, by contrast. No statement anywhere locates a word stress or accent position in Ogba.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about suprasegmental morphology (suprafixes) at word level in a contrastive Ogba-English study by a native-speaker linguist; it is not a phonological description and gives no phonetic detail on prominence. Supporting first-hand tone-only descriptions: Blench 2013 p.i; Williamson/Blench/Ohiri-Aniche 2013 sec. 5.3 p.2; Nwokoji 2024 p.210 ('Ọgba is a tonal language').
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Ogba of Ogba/Egbema/Ndoni LGA, Rivers State (dialects named Egni/Egnih, Igburu, and others; Nwokoji 2024 and Eme 1993 focus on the Egni dialect; Blench's dictionary is the Ọmọkụ-based Ogba Language Committee's). Glottolog's two 'descriptive' references (Maduagwu 2006; Maduagwu & Obiamalu 2016) concern the 'Ògbahù dialect of Ìgbò', which by name and framing looks like an Igbo town lect rather than Igboid Ogba [ogc]; this assignment was not verifiable here and should be checked before those works are pursued.

tone_statements.quote: O̩gba is a tone language. In other words, tones are extremely significant in the grammar of the language. ... This entails that tones are phonemic in the O̩gba language. ... Ahiamadu (2000) and Isaac (2018) say that O̩gba has high tone ( ʹ ), low tone ( ˋ ), high-low ( ˆ ), and mid-tone ( ˉ ). They unanimously recommend that as a convention, all the mid tones ( ˉ ) should be left unmarked in O̩gba. In view of that, any data presented in the O̩gba language with an unmarked tone in this paper should be read as mid.
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone, phonemic: H, L, HL (falling) plus a 'mid' (= downstepped H in Blench's description) left unmarked in the local convention; no stress mentioned.

tone_statements.quote: Suprafix And Superfix: In a tonal language like Ọgba i.e. language were a variation in the pitch of the voice causes a change in meaning between segmental identical utterances such as Ọgba. A tone is a meaning– making element in some language. It is a systematic variation of the voice pitch used by language to distinguish, both lexical and grammatical meanings. Ọgba is a tonal language, and all its major dialects, such as Egni̩ and Igburu. In Ọgba, the tone carried by a word is an essential feature of its meaning a). íshí→ head, íshì → ordour, ìshì → blindness, íshí →to cook b). íkné → strength, íkè → to share, íké → to tie ìké → bunch c). òké → rat, ókè → boundary, òkè → share d) égwù → butock égwú → song ègwù → tilapia [narrow table column; line breaks collapsed, spelling as printed]

sources.note: Calls Ọgba 'a tonal language' (p.346) and justifies the sub-dotted vowel letters by 'tones' with one pair aznu 'back' / ạznu 'fish' (p.351); proposes a 29-letter alphabet with no tone-marking convention and gives no tone inventory.
